strings.title: Dividing Fractions by Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing by a fraction asks "how many of these fit?": 3/4 ÷ 1/8 is how many eighths fit in three quarters. Use the number line to count the jumps.
strings.keywords: how many fit, groups of, quotative division, common denominator, number line
watchFor: Expecting the answer to be smaller than the first number: ask "How many quarters fit in a half?"
Dividing numerators and denominators without meaning: ask "What is the question really asking?"
Losing the leftover part in 5/6 ÷ 1/3: ask "After 2 thirds, what's left? What part of a third is it?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 1/2 ÷ 1/4 bigger than 1/2?" Land: dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit, and lots of small pieces can fit. When the pieces share a denominator, just count them.

problems.notes: Look for: two quarters fit in a half. Ask: "How many quarters fit in a half?" Word choice: "how many 1/4s fit in 1/2". Model: numberline 0 +1/4x2

responses.say: Two quarters make a half, so 2.
responses.tip: The target meaning: how many fit.
Same denominator, then divide the counts.
Multiplied instead. Ask: how many quarters fit in a half?

problems.notes: Look for: 3/4 is 6/8, so 6 eighths fit. Ask: "What's 3/4 in eighths?" Model: numberline 0 +1/8x6

responses.say: Six eighths fit in three quarters.

responses.tip: Ask: is 3/32 how many eighths fit, or a tiny piece?

problems.notes: Look for: 2/3 = 4/6. Ask: "How is this like the last one?" Model: numberline 0 +1/6x4

responses.say: Four sixths fit in two thirds.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 thirds fit, with 1/6 left, which is half a third. Ask: "What's left over? How much of a third is it?" Model: numberline 0 +1/3x2 +1/6

responses.say: Two thirds fit, and the 1/6 left is half a third. 2 1/2.
responses.tip: Ask: why is the leftover a half, not a sixth?
Common denominators, then divide the counts.
Named the leftover in sixths. Ask: what part of a third is 1/6?

problems.notes: Look for: four 3/4 jumps make 3. Ask: "How many three-quarters fit in 3?" Model: numberline 0 +3/4x4

responses.tip: Multiplied. Ask: should the answer be more or less than 3?

problems.notes: Look for: 3/4 doesn't fit in 2/3 even once, so less than 1: 8/12 ÷ 9/12 = 8/9. Ask: "Does 3/4 fit into 2/3 a whole time?" Model: text 2/3 = 8/12 ; 3/4 = 9/12 ; 8/12 ÷ 9/12 = 8/9

responses.tip: Common denominators again.
Multiply by the reciprocal. Ask: why does it match?
Flipped the wrong fraction. Ask: is 3/4 bigger than 2/3? So does it fit more than once?

strings.title: Multiplying Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Multiplying fractions finds a part of a part. On the area model, the denominators tell the size of each little piece and the numerators tell how many pieces overlap.
strings.keywords: of, part of a part, area model, overlap, numerator, denominator
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators: ask "Is half of a third more or less than a third?"
Making a common denominator first out of habit: ask "Do we need the same size pieces to multiply?"
Forgetting to simplify, or not seeing an easier way (5/6 × 3/4): ask "Could you simplify first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is the answer smaller than both fractions?" Land: it's a part of a part. Multiply denominators to get the piece size, numerators to count the overlap.

problems.notes: Look for: half of a third. Ask: "How many pieces make the whole?" Word choice: "one half of one third". Model: area 1/2 x 1/3

responses.say: Half of a third is a sixth.

responses.tip: Added. Ask: is half of a third more than a third?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 3 fourths is 3 eighths. Ask: "What size are the pieces now?" Model: area 1/2 x 3/4
Look for: a quarter of 3 quarters. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: area 1/4 x 3/4

responses.tip: Half of 3/8 is 3/16.
Added. Ask: a quarter of something less than 1, is it a half?

problems.notes: Look for: 6/15 = 2/5. Ask: "Can you simplify?" Model: area 2/3 x 3/5

responses.tip: A nice shortcut. Ask: why does it work?

problems.notes: Look for: 6/20 = 3/10. Ask: "What do the denominators tell you?" Model: area 3/4 x 2/5

responses.tip: Flipped as if dividing. Ask: is 3/4 of 2/5 more than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 15/24 = 5/8, or simplify 3 and 6 first. Ask: "Could you simplify first?" Model: area 5/6 x 3/4

responses.say: Swap the denominators: 5/4 × 3/6, and 3/6 is 1/2. So 5/8.
responses.tip: Simplifying first. Ask: why can we swap the denominators?

problems.notes: Look for: 1 × 1/3 + 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/3 + 1/6. Ask: "Can you split the mixed number?" Model: area 1 1/2 x 1/3

responses.tip: Switching the order.
Multiplied only the fraction part. Ask: what is 1 × 1/3?

strings.title: Adding Unlike Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To add or subtract fractions with different denominators, rename them as the same-sized pieces. Minutes on a clock make twelfths, sixths, fourths and thirds easy.
strings.keywords: common denominator, equivalent fractions, twelfths, minutes, clock, rename
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5): ask "Is 2/5 more or less than 1/2?"
Renaming only one fraction: ask "Are both fractions the same-sized pieces now?"
Getting lost when the sum goes past 1: ask "How many minutes past the hour?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does the clock work so well for these?" Land: 60 minutes splits evenly into halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and twelfths, so every fraction becomes minutes. In fractions, that's finding a common denominator.

problems.notes: Look for: 30 + 20 = 50 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is a half? A third?" Word choice: "same-sized pieces". Model: clock 1/2 + 1/3

responses.say: 30 + 20 = 50 minutes, which is 5/6 of an hour.
responses.tip: Ask: how is 50 minutes 5/6?
Common denominator.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 2/5 more than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. Ask: "What are 35 minutes as a fraction?" Model: clock 1/4 + 1/3
Look for: 40 + 15 = 55 minutes. Ask: "How close to an hour?" Model: clock 2/3 + 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: 2/3 plus a bit more, can it be less than a half?

problems.notes: Look for: 45 + 40 = 85 minutes, an hour and 25. Ask: "What happens past the hour?" Model: clock 3/4 + 2/3
Look for: 50 − 15 = 35 minutes. Ask: "Does subtracting work the same way?" Model: clock 5/6 - 1/4

responses.tip: Subtracted tops and bottoms. Ask: can the answer be 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 90 − 40 = 50 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is 1 1/2 hours?" Model: clock 1 1/2 - 2/3

responses.tip: Through the whole number.

problems.notes: Look for: tenths, not minutes: 6/10 + 5/10. Ask: "Does the clock work for fifths? What could you use instead?" Model: text 3/5 = 6/10 ; 1/2 = 5/10 ; 6/10 + 5/10 = 11/10 = 1 1/10

responses.tip: Tenths are the common piece.
Decimals: also tenths.
Ask: 3/5 plus a half, can it be less than 1?

strings.title: Mixed Numbers with Different Denominators
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Add or subtract mixed numbers by jumping through whole numbers on the number line, renaming fractions as the same-sized pieces when you need to.
strings.keywords: mixed number, whole number, common denominator, jump through a whole, rename
watchFor: Subtracting the parts separately in 3 1/4 − 1 1/2 (2 −1/4): ask "Can you take 1/2 from 1/4? What could you jump to first?"
Adding the fractions without a common denominator: ask "Are halves and thirds the same size?"
Losing the whole numbers: ask "Did you take away the 1 as well as the fraction?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did jumping to a whole number help?" Land: break the jump into the whole part and pieces that land on whole numbers. Rename fractions only when the pieces don't match.

problems.notes: Look for: back 1/4 to 3, then 1/4 more. Ask: "How is 1/2 made of quarters?" Word choice: "jump to the whole number". Model: numberline 3 1/4 -1/4 -1/4

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Renaming a whole.
Ask: did anything get taken away?

problems.notes: Look for: back 1, then the same as the last one. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 3 1/4 -1 -1/4 -1/4

responses.say: Back 1 to 2 1/4, back 1/4 to 2, back 1/4 more: 1 3/4.

responses.tip: Used the last problem.
Subtracted 1/4 from 1/2 instead. Ask: should the answer be less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: back 1, back 1/2 to 1, then 1/3 more. Ask: "What is 5/6 made of?" Model: numberline 2 1/2 -1 -1/2 -1/3

responses.tip: Subtracted the fractions backward. Ask: is 1 5/6 more than 1 1/2? So less than 1 is left.

problems.notes: Look for: 1 2/3 + 2 = 3 2/3, + 1/3 = 4, + 1/6. Ask: "What does 3 2/3 need to make 4?" Model: numberline 1 2/3 +2 +1/3 +1/6

responses.tip: Clock for the fraction parts: 40 + 30 = 70 minutes.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 2/3 + 1/2 more or less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: back 2, back 1/3 to 2, then 5/12 more. Ask: "What's 3/4 − 1/3 in twelfths?" Model: numberline 4 1/3 -2 -1/3 -5/12

responses.say: Back 2 to 2 1/3, back 1/3 to 2, back 5/12 more: 1 7/12.

problems.notes: Look for: back 2 to 3, then 3/8 to 2 5/8. Ask: "Could you count up from 2 3/8?" Model: numberline 2 3/8 >3 >5

responses.tip: Counting up.
Ask: 5 − 2 is 3. Then take away 3/8 more: more or less than 3?
